lesson.title: Gases, pressure and the air receiver

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the pressure line running back to zero pressure at absolute zero, and pV ÷ T holding steady only in absolute units, when you drag the heat with the piston locked.
interactive.title: The sealed cylinder
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: The lesson runs over thirteen small screens. The main picture is a sealed cylinder of gas under a piston. A heater sits beneath it, and one gauge gives two readings. Gauge pressure is how far the gas is above the atmosphere, or below it. Absolute pressure is gauge plus the atmosphere, taken as 1 bar. So absolute pressure counts from no push at all. Where a screen lets you, one slider moves the piston, setting the volume from 1 to 6 L. It opens at 3 L. Another sets the heater's temperature, from 0 to 150 °C. It opens at 27 °C, which is 300 K. The gas starts at 2 bar absolute, 1 bar gauge. Each screen sets the piston one of three ways: free to move, locked, or floating under a steady load. Locked holds the volume. Floating holds the pressure, so warming pushes the piston up. On some screens the heater holds the temperature instead. A tag beside the cylinder always names what is held. Two charts follow the gas as a dot. The first plots absolute pressure, 0 to 10 bar, against volume, 0 to 6 L. With the temperature held, the dot runs along a curve where pressure × volume stays the same. So half the volume gives twice the pressure. The second plots absolute pressure against temperature in °C, from −300 to 200 °C. With the piston locked, the dot runs along a straight line. An Extend button carries that line on, dashed. It runs down to zero pressure at −273 °C, absolute zero. Kelvin are counted from there: K = °C + 273. A box shows pV ÷ T, with a three-way choice of units. In absolute pressure and kelvin it reads 0.020 bar·L/K at the start, 2 × 3 ÷ 300. It stays there whatever changes. In gauge pressure and kelvin it starts at 1 × 3 ÷ 300 = 0.010. Pushing the piston to 1.5 L sends it to 0.015, in red. In absolute pressure and °C it starts at 2 × 3 ÷ 27, about 0.222. Warming to 127 °C with the piston locked takes the gas to about 2.67 bar absolute. The box then reads about 0.063, in red. On a phone the three readouts wrap onto two rows. On the last screens, a 500 L air receiver and its compressor take the cylinder's place. The compressor cuts in at 6 bar gauge and cuts out at 8 bar gauge. That is 7 and 9 bar absolute, and the band between them is shaded on the gauge. Let out at 1 bar, the receiver's air at 9 bar absolute would fill 500 × 9 = 4,500 L. At 7 bar it fills 3,500 L. So the band gives 1,000 L, shown in a readout. At an example draw of 250 L a minute, the compressor stays off for 1,000 ÷ 250 = 4 minutes. A switch doubles the receiver to 1,000 L. Its band holds 2,000 L and lasts 8 minutes. So the motor starts half as often. Screen by screen. Screen 1 is a warm-up sum. 2 L of gas at 3 bar absolute is pushed into 1 L at the same temperature. What is its pressure? The choices are 6 bar, 1.5 bar or 4 bar absolute. A right answer says Still there. Screen 2 says what pressure is, force ÷ area in pascals, with 1 bar as 100 kPa. It shows the gauge's two readings and Boyle's law on the cylinder. With the temperature held, 3 L at 2 bar absolute pushed to 1.5 L reads 4 bar absolute, 3 bar gauge. Screen 3 asks what a gauge reading 3 bar shows after the volume is halved at the same temperature: 6 bar, 7 bar or 8 bar. Screen 4 shows the piston locked while the heater warms the gas from 27 °C to 127 °C. The pressure line is straight, and Extend runs it to zero at −273 °C. That is the pressure law. 300 K to 400 K is a third more, so 2 bar becomes about 2.67 bar. Screen 5 asks about a locked cylinder at 2 bar absolute and 20 °C, warmed to 40 °C: about 2.1 bar, 4 bar or 2 bar absolute. Screen 6 shows the piston floating under a steady load. Warming from 27 °C to 127 °C, 300 K to 400 K, leaves the pressure at 2 bar absolute. The volume grows from 3 L to 4 L. That is Charles's law. Screen 7 asks what happens when the gas warms from 300 K to 450 K with the piston floating. One choice: the pressure stays the same and the volume grows by half. Another: the pressure rises by half and the volume stays the same. The last: both rise. Screen 8 shows the pV ÷ T box steady in absolute units while the piston moves and the gas warms. For the last second the box switches to gauge pressure, and it drifts, in red. In °C it drifts too. Screen 9 asks about gas at 1 bar absolute, 6 L and 27 °C, pushed to 2 L and heated to 127 °C: 4 bar, 3 bar or about 14 bar absolute. Screen 10 shows the receiver and its band. The bigger receiver lasts twice as long. Screens 11, 12 and 13 mix it all. Screen 11: a 300 L receiver runs between 6 and 8 bar gauge. How much air at atmospheric pressure does it give from cut-out to cut-in? 600 L, 2,700 L or 300 L. Screen 12: a receiver at 7 bar gauge and 20 °C warms to 50 °C. What does its gauge read? About 7.8 bar, 17.5 bar or about 8.8 bar. Screen 13: a receiver falls from 8 to 6 bar gauge at a steady temperature. What share of its air has gone? About 22%, 25% or about 78%. On screens 11 and 13 a row of faint blocks waits below the picture, and fills in once the answer is right. Where it can, a wrong pick is drawn on the charts or the box, so you see where it fails.
interactive.ignores: The gas is treated as an ideal gas. Real gases stray from the straight line at very high pressures and near the point where they turn to liquid. So no real gas reaches zero pressure at absolute zero. The dashed line is the straight line carried on, not a measurement. The atmosphere is taken as 1 bar. A real one is about 1.01 bar, and it changes with the weather and with height. A quick squeeze warms a gas, and a quick expansion against the piston cools it. Here the heater holds whatever temperature is locked, as if each move were made slowly. The piston has no friction, and the cylinder never leaks. A real receiver also collects water from the air, which has to be drained off.

explain.text:
A trapped gas pushes on every wall around it. Squeeze it or warm it, and that push changes in simple proportion. The catch is where you count from. The rule only works when pressure and temperature are counted from true zero. Picture the push as the gas's molecules striking the walls. Halve the space and they strike each bit of wall twice as often. Warm them and they strike harder and more often.

Pressure is force ÷ area. Its unit is the pascal, one newton on each square metre, the same unit as stress. 1 bar is 100 kPa, about the push of the atmosphere. A pressure gauge open to the air reads zero. Yet the air is pushing on it at about 1 bar. So a gauge reads how far you are above the atmosphere, or below it. That is [[gauge pressure]]. Add the atmosphere and you get [[absolute pressure]], counted from no push at all.[^1] Now hold a gas's temperature and halve its volume. Its pressure doubles.[^2] That is Boyle's law. But it is the absolute pressure that doubles. A gauge reading 1 bar means the gas pushes with 2 bar in all. The gauge just leaves out the atmosphere's share. Halve the volume and the gas pushes with 4 bar absolute. So the gauge now reads 3 bar, not 2.

Temperature has the same trap. Lock the piston so the volume cannot change, then warm the gas. Its pressure climbs in a straight line. Carry that line on to colder and colder gas. It reaches zero pressure at about −273 °C. That is absolute zero, where the kelvin scale starts. So with the volume held, pressure is in proportion to the kelvin temperature, not the Celsius one.[^3] That is the pressure law. Warm a locked cylinder from 20 °C to 40 °C. The Celsius figure doubles. But 293 K to 313 K is only about 7% more. So the absolute pressure rises about 7%.

What happens also depends on what is held. Take 3 L of gas at 2 bar absolute, and let the piston float under a steady load. Warm the gas from 300 K to 400 K. The pressure stays the same. The 3 L grows to 4 L, in step with the kelvin temperature. That is Charles's law. Put the laws together. Pressure is in proportion to kelvin, and in inverse proportion to volume. So for the same trapped gas, when all three change, pV ÷ T stays the same in absolute units: p₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂V₂ ÷ T₂. Take a receiver at 7 bar gauge and 20 °C that warms to 50 °C. Its volume is held. It starts at 8 bar absolute. It ends at 8 × 323 ÷ 293, about 8.8 bar absolute. So its gauge reads about 7.8 bar. Do the same sum in gauge and Celsius, and it says 17.5 bar. That would more than double the pressure for 30 °C of warming. It is nonsense.

pV ÷ T also measures how much gas there is. For a mass m of gas, pV = mRT, with p in pascals, V in m³ and T in kelvin. R is a constant for each gas. For air it is 287 J/(kg K). So a 1 m³ receiver at 800 kPa absolute and 20 °C holds 800,000 ÷ (287 × 293) kg. That is about 9.5 kg of air. As a check, air at 100 kPa and 15 °C works out at about 1.21 kg in each m³. Measured air at sea level is about 1.23 kg/m³, close to it. So in a receiver at a steady temperature, the amount of air follows the absolute pressure.

An [[air receiver]] stores air the compressor has already made. The compressor cuts in at a low pressure and cuts out at a high one. Between starts, only the air in that band gets used. Say a 500 L receiver runs between 6 and 8 bar gauge. That is 7 and 9 bar absolute. By Boyle's law, its air at 9 bar would fill 4,500 L at 1 bar. At 7 bar it fills 3,500 L. So the band gives 1,000 L. The band is the same 2 bar wide in gauge or absolute. A difference does not care where you count from. A ratio does. Double the receiver and the band holds twice the air, so the motor starts less often.[^4] Each start draws the motor's starting current. A common sizing rule asks for at least 2 minutes of compressor running to fill the band, with no air drawn off. A higher pressure does not give more flow. Raise the pressure, and the compressor delivers less air.[^5] Water also settles out of the air in a receiver, and it has to be drained.[^6] All of this treats the air as an ideal gas, a simplified model. Real gases stray from it at very high pressures and near the point where they turn to liquid.

**Pressure, volume and temperature are in proportion only when counted from true zero. So before any gas sum, add the atmosphere to a gauge reading and 273 to a Celsius one.**

analogy.text: Picture a voltmeter that takes 100 V off every reading. A 440 V supply shows 340. Read two points at 440 V and 430 V, and it shows 340 and 330. They are still 10 apart, because the offset cancels in a difference. But ask whether one voltage is twice another, and the meter gets it wrong. A pressure gauge is that meter, with the atmosphere as its offset. Celsius is that meter for temperature, with 273 as its offset.
analogy.breaks: Voltage has no true zero. Every voltage is a difference between two points, so choosing your reference loses nothing. Pressure and temperature do have a true zero, with nothing below it. The gas laws are written from there. And the atmosphere is not a fixed offset. It changes with the weather and with height.

practice.text:
Before work on a receiver or its pipework, isolate it from the compressor and vent it fully to the open air.[^7] A gauge shows that pressure is there, but not that all of it has gone. So confirm zero pressure at an open vent before you break into the system.[^8]

- Write down what is held: the volume, the temperature or the pressure.
- Turn every gauge pressure into absolute: add the atmosphere, about 1 bar.
- Turn every Celsius temperature into kelvin: add 273.
- Use p₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂V₂ ÷ T₂, and cancel whatever is held.
- If a gauge will show the answer, take the atmosphere off again.

**Rules of thumb:** A difference comes out the same in gauge or absolute, and in °C or kelvin. A ratio needs absolute pressure and kelvin. Near room temperature, about 300 K, each 3 °C of warming adds about 1% to a sealed vessel's absolute pressure.

**Worked example:** A receiver reads 7 bar gauge at 20 °C, and the space around it warms to 50 °C. In absolute units it starts at 8 bar and 293 K, and goes to 323 K. The volume is held. So the pressure goes to 8 × 323 ÷ 293, about 8.8 bar absolute. The gauge reads about 7.8 bar.

**Common mistakes**
- Putting a gauge reading into a ratio. At a steady temperature, halving the volume from 1 bar gauge gives 3 bar gauge, not 2.
- Putting Celsius into a ratio. Warming a sealed vessel from 20 °C to 40 °C raises its absolute pressure about 7%. It does not double it.
- Thinking warming always raises the pressure. It does when the volume is held. With a floating piston, the volume grows instead.
- Counting all of a receiver's air as usable between starts. Only the air in the band between cut-in and cut-out is.

interactive.html:
A trapped gas, then an air receiver, each with one gauge that reads two ways. Every figure is an example.

An ideal gas. The atmosphere is taken as 1 bar, and absolute zero as −273 °C.
interactive.title: The sealed cylinder
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the pressure line running back to zero pressure at absolute zero, and pV ÷ T holding steady only in absolute units, when you drag the heat with the piston locked.

checks.label: Absolute pressure is gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure, on every screen and setting
Compressed into half its volume at a steady temperature, the gas's pressure doubles
The pressure of the trapped gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature while the volume does not change, so its line meets zero pressure at absolute zero
A bigger receiver means less frequent motor starts: twice the receiver holds twice the air in its band and keeps the compressor off twice as long

Every number the screens print comes from the rule: 6, 1.5 and 4 bar; 4 bar absolute, 3 gauge and 2; 6, 7 and 8 bar; 450 K and 4.5 L; 300 L, 2,700, 2,100 and 600 L; 293 K, 313 K and 7%; about 2.1 bar against 4; 400 K and 4 L; 0.020, 0.010, 0.015, 0.222, 2.67 and 0.063; 4, 3 and about 14 bar; 7 and 9 bar absolute, 4,500, 3,500 and 1,000 L, 4 minutes, 2,000 L and 8 minutes; 8 bar, 323 K, about 8.8 and 7.8 bar against 17.5; about 22%, 25% and 78%
pV ÷ T holds at 0.020 in absolute pressure and kelvin wherever the piston and heater go; in gauge it goes from 0.010 to 0.015 at 1.5 L, and in °C from 0.222 to 0.063 at 127 °C
With the piston floating, 27 °C to 127 °C keeps 2 bar absolute and takes 3 L to 4 L; locked, the same warming takes 2 bar to about 2.67
The readings follow the piston and the heat at once, and the receiver starts at 8 bar gauge and falls to 6 bar in 4 minutes
Each puzzle offers three different answers including its right one, every wrong answer has its own hint, and before Check nothing on its picture shows the answer or a red mark

A wrong pick is drawn in red where it fails: 1.5 and 4 bar off the curve; the gauge doubled or read as absolute; 4 bar counted from 0 °C and no change; the locked and both-up points; heat left out and 14 bar off the chart; all of it and one tankful; 8.8 read as gauge and 17.5 from 0 °C; 2 of 8 and what is left. A right answer draws no red

A right answer draws the rule's result: 6 bar at 1 L; 8 bar absolute on the gauge; about 2.14 bar at 40 °C; 4.5 L at 2 bar; 4 bar at 2 L; the band's two blocks; about 8.82 bar absolute at 50 °C; 2 of 9 parts gone at 7 bar absolute
Every demonstration has finished within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2 s
Every demonstration screen keeps to about 90 words

applied.problem: A gauge can read below the atmosphere (the cylinder at 6 L and 0 °C is about 0.91 bar absolute; pump suction in i8); the 7% rise is in absolute pressure only, a gauge rises about 14%; pV ÷ T stays fixed only for the same trapped gas; halving space doubles strikes per bit of wall, not per molecule.

Isolation should be locked off and venting confirmed, not taken from a gauge alone; the 7% mistake must say absolute pressure in a sealed vessel (a gauge reading rises more), and the halving example holds only at a steady temperature.
Gauge pressure can be below the atmosphere: at 6 L and 0 °C, within the sliders' range, the gas is about 0.91 bar absolute, so the gauge reads about −0.09 bar.

notes.problem: The heater slider reaches 0 °C, where the pV ÷ T box's absolute-and-°C option divides by zero; the build must show that case sensibly, for instance as no answer, rather than Infinity or NaN.
